substantiveFindings: Verified all four input blobs at staging 7cdf8f42 and in the working tree (extraction 47,349 bytes). Pinned validators pass; the date receipt is hash-current, status research-blocked, with one blanket finding over all 60 items.
Read all 204 units (Treatise on Carriages and Dress, part two) in both English fields. Accepted repairs r0001 (s0066) and r0002 (s0150) are present in the source.

English: 24 definite field repairs across 17 units. Mistranslations: 翬翟/榮華 (pheasants and blossoms, not kingfishers and sable), 爵頭色 (sparrow-head color), 大難 = 大儺 (the Great Exorcism, not a crisis), 中黃門童子佩刀 (the pages' girdle-knife, not boys given as gifts), 繆織 (interwoven, not "wrongly"), the s0195 reversed ending, the s0146 invented "summer face", and the s0149 numeric error (29.9 chi is nearly thirty feet, not three yards). Attribution/name errors: the s0005 "tailors" and the s0052 "he" (Confucius); "Marquis Huiwen" for 趙惠文 (King Huiwen of Zhao); "Shi clan cap" for 術氏冠; "Zhao’s martial king"; and "Kings of blood", a repeat of the wording accepted repair r0002 already removed at s0150.

Chronology: 56 of 60 items verify as correct era conversions, reign or career containing bounds, or legendary qualitative hints; two of these (Duke of Zhou and King Cheng, BC 1042-) are conventional reconstructions kept with explicit uncertainty. Four concrete defects: claim-38 dates 高祖微時 (before Gaozu's rising) to the post-rising BC 209-206 window; claim-45 invents a BC 400 start for 楚王嘗獲之; claim-46 merges the unnamed xiezhi king with the ruler Qin conquered in BC 223; and claim-52 dates Zi Zang of Zheng to BC 580-570, contradicting the cited Zuo Commentary (Duke Xi 24, 636 BC). A native date-repair proposal makes these four items undated or removes them and empties the two dependent hints.

Identity and mentions: p015 merges two unidentified Chu rulers (s0066 vs the 其君 of s0068); the proposal retracts the s0068 defeated-ruler claim and removes s0068 from p015's name and role evidence. p016 carries an unsupported title name "Marquis Huiwen", replaced by the personal name "Zhao Huiwen". The s0066 English mention span covered a whole clause and is narrowed to "the king of Chu". The s0099 mention follows the name repair. No new people or missing mentions were found; no merges or canonical identifications are proposed.

The fully combined candidate passes the native extraction validator in memory, after the native input refresh and reconciliation of 10 preflight English candidates, with no chronology geometry errors. Candidate extraction sha256:2df06d49884403ffe7047cc0be9830e12f6688c9c63060bae623baa932bd608f.

definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Mianguan (crown cap), changguan (long cap), weimaoguan (deferential-appearance cap), pibianguan (leather-skullcap), juebianguan (noble-skullcap), tongtianguan (pierce-heaven cap), yuanyouguan (far-roaming cap), gaoshanguan (high-mountain cap), jinxianguan (advance-the-worthy cap), faguan (law cap), wuguan (martial cap), jianhuaguan (splendid-bloom cap), fangshanguan (square-mountain cap), qiaoshiguan (ingenious-gentleman cap), quefeiguan (repel-wrong cap), quediguan (repel-enemy cap), Fan Kuai cap, Shu clan cap, heguan (pheasant cap), ze (kerchief), pei (pendants), dao (sword), yin (seal), yellow-red ribbon, red ribbon, green ribbon, purple ribbon, blue-green ribbon, black ribbon, yellow ribbon, blue-black twisted cord, and attire of the empress and consorts.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 術氏冠 is read Shù-shì; "Shi" is not a reading of 術. Use the same romanization at s0091.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 後世聖人易之以絲麻，觀翬翟之文，榮華之色，乃染帛以效之，始作五采，成以爲服。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Later sages replaced these with silk and hemp; observing the patterns of kingfisher and sable and the splendor of their colors, they dyed fabrics to imitate them, first devised the five hues, and completed them as garments.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Later sages replaced these with silk and hemp; observing the markings of variegated pheasants and the colors of flowering plants, they dyed fabrics to imitate them, first devised the five hues, and completed them as garments.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 翬翟 are two kinds of variegated pheasant (翬 five-colored, 翟 long-tailed), and 榮華 means blossoms/flowering plants. The source mentions neither kingfishers nor sable.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 後世聖人易之以絲麻，觀翬翟之文，榮華之色，乃染帛以效之，始作五采，成以爲服。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Later sages introduced silk and linen, took inspiration from the plumage of kingfishers and the sheen of costly furs, dyed cloth to match those colors, and so established the five-color system that became formal dress.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Later sages introduced silk and linen, took inspiration from the markings of pheasants and the colors of blossoms, dyed cloth to match those colors, and so established the five-color system that became formal dress.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: Same source error as the literal field: 翬翟 are pheasants and 榮華 are blossoms, not kingfishers and costly furs.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 見鳥獸有冠角髯胡之製，遂作冠冕纓蕤，以爲首飾。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Noting how birds and beasts wore crests, horns, and beards by nature, tailors fashioned caps and crowns with hanging tassels as deliberate head ornaments.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Noting how birds and beasts wore crests, horns, and beards by nature, the sages fashioned caps and crowns with hanging tassels as deliberate head ornaments.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: The subject continues from s0004 後世聖人 (later sages): 遂作冠冕纓蕤. The source has no tailors, so the idiomatic field reassigns the sages' act.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 遂作冠冕纓蕤，以爲首飾

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 廣八寸，長尺二寸，如爵形，前小後大，繒其上似爵頭色，有收持笄，所謂夏收殷冔者也。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Eight inches wide, one foot two inches long, shaped like a jue-vessel, small in front and large in back; silk on top in the color of a jue’s lip; it has a pin to secure it—what are called the Xia shou and Yin xu styles.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Eight inches wide, one foot two inches long, shaped like a jue-vessel, small in front and large in back; silk over the top in the color of a sparrow’s head; it has a pin to secure it—what are called the Xia shou and Yin xu styles.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 爵頭色 is the color of a sparrow's head (爵 = 雀, a dark reddish color from which the juebian takes its name). It is not a vessel's lip.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 廣八寸，長尺二寸，如爵形，前小後大，繒其上似爵頭色，有收持笄，所謂夏收殷冔者也。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: It measured eight by twelve inches, flared like a bronze jue, dyed on the crown to suggest a cup’s rim, and fastened with a hairpin—the forms antiquity knew as the Xia shou and Shang xu caps.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: It measured eight by twelve inches, flared like a bronze jue, covered on top with silk the dark red of a sparrow’s head, and fastened with a hairpin—the forms antiquity knew as the Xia shou and Shang xu caps.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 繒其上似爵頭色 describes silk over the top in sparrow-head color, not dye suggesting a cup rim.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 縫掖其袖，合而縫大之，近今袍者也。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: He stitched the sleeves at the armpit, joining and enlarging them; it is close to the robes of today.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Its sleeves are seamed at the armpit, joined and sewn large; it is close to the robes of today.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 縫掖其袖，合而縫大之 describes how the fengye garment is made. There is no subject "he", and Confucius (s0051) is not said to have sewn anything.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 侍中、中常侍加黃金璫，附蟬爲文，貂尾爲飾，謂之「趙惠文冠」。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Palace attendants and regular palace attendants add a gold knob, cicada pattern in front, and sable tail as ornament; it is called the “Marquis Huiwen cap.”
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Palace attendants and regular palace attendants add a gold knob, cicada pattern in front, and sable tail as ornament; it is called the “Zhao Huiwen cap.”
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 趙惠文冠 names Huiwen of Zhao, i.e. King Huiwen of Zhao (the extraction's p016). The source has no "Marquis", and he was a king.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 侍中、中常侍加黃金璫，附蟬爲文，貂尾爲飾，謂之「趙惠文冠」。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Palace attendants gilded the cap with a front cicada plaque and sable tail—hence the nickname “Marquis Huiwen crown.”
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Palace attendants gilded the cap with a front cicada plaque and sable tail—hence the name “Zhao Huiwen crown.”
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: Same error as the literal field: 趙惠文 is King Huiwen of Zhao, not a marquis.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 建武時，匈奴內屬，世祖賜南單於衣服，以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀云。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: In the Jianwu era, when the Xiongnu submitted, the Founding Emperor granted the Southern Chanyu clothing, with the attendant’s Huiwen cap and yellow-gate lads with girdle swords, it is said.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: In the Jianwu era, when the Xiongnu submitted, the Founding Emperor granted the Southern Chanyu clothing, namely the Huiwen cap of the Regular Palace Attendants and the girdle-knife of the Inner Yellow Gate pages, it is said.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀 lists items of dress: a Huiwen cap of the Regular Palace Attendants' type and the girdle-knife of the Inner Yellow Gate pages. No boys were given to the Chanyu.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀云

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 建武時，匈奴內屬，世祖賜南單於衣服，以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀云。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: When the Southern Chanyu came in during Jianwu, Guangwu presented him with court dress that included the golden cicada cap and yellow-gate boys with ritual swords.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: When the Southern Chanyu came in during Jianwu, Guangwu presented him with court dress that included the Regular Palace Attendants’ Huiwen cap and the girdle-knife worn by Inner Yellow Gate pages.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: The idiomatic field presents "yellow-gate boys" as a gift; the source gives the pages' girdle-knife (中黃門童子佩刀). It also replaces the named Huiwen cap of the Regular Palace Attendants (中常侍惠文冠) with an unattested "golden cicada cap".

sourceWitness.excerpt: 以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀云

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 司馬殿門大難，衛士服之。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: At the great crisis at the Sima Gate, guards wear it.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: At the Great Exorcism (大難, i.e. 大儺) at the Sima palace gates, the guards wear it.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 司馬殿門大難 refers to the year-end Great Exorcism (難 read nuó = 儺), a palace rite in which the guards took part. It is not a crisis or emergency.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 司馬殿門大難，衛士服之

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 司馬殿門大難，衛士服之。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Guards donned it during the Sima Gate emergency.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Guards wore it at the Sima palace gates during the Great Exorcism.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 大難 here is the Great Exorcism ritual (大儺), not an emergency.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 司馬殿門大難，衛士服之

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 術氏冠，前圓，吳制，差池邐迤四重，趙武靈王好服之。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: The Shi clan cap is round in front, a Wu style, rippling in four layers; King Wuling of Zhao loved to wear it.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: The Shu clan cap is round in front, a Wu style, rippling in four layers; King Wuling of Zhao loved to wear it.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 術氏冠 is read Shù-shì; "Shi" is not a reading of 術 (same fix as s0001).

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 術氏冠，前圓，吳制，差池邐迤四重，趙武靈王好服之。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: The Shi-style round Wu cap, tiered in four rippling layers, was a favorite of King Wuling of Zhao.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: The Shu clan’s round Wu-style cap, tiered in four rippling layers, was a favorite of King Wuling of Zhao.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 術氏冠 is read Shù-shì, not Shi; this also restores the clan-name sense of 術氏.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 鶡者，勇雉也，其鬥對一死乃止，故趙武靈王以表武士，秦施之焉。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: The fighting cock-pheasant dies rather than yield, so Zhao’s martial king and later Qin used its plumes to brand elite troops.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: The fighting cock-pheasant dies rather than yield, so King Wuling of Zhao and later Qin used its plumes to mark out their warriors.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 趙武靈王 is King Wuling of Zhao, as both English fields render it at s0071 and s0091. "Zhao’s martial king" turns his posthumous name into a description. 以表武士 means to mark warriors, not to brand elite troops.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 故趙武靈王以表武士，秦施之焉

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 罷廟，侍御史任方奏請非乘從時，皆冠一梁，不宜以爲常服。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: After the imperial shrines closed, Censor Ren Fang urged that the single-ridged cap be reserved for processional duty and not treated as everyday wear.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: After the temple visits ended, Censor Ren Fang urged that the single-ridged cap be reserved for processional duty and not treated as everyday wear.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 罷廟 means the temple visit (s0100) ended. The shrines did not close.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 韨佩既廢，秦乃以採組連結於璲，光明章表，轉相結受，故謂之綬。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Qin replaced jade sets with bright silk cords knotted to seal-stones—origin of the named “ribbon” (shou).
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Qin replaced jade sets with bright silk cords knotted to the sui jade pieces—origin of the named “ribbon” (shou).
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 璲 are the jade pendant links kept in s0130 (留其係璲) and glossed at s0158 (古佩璲). They are not seal-stones; the seals come in only at s0133.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 諸侯王黃金錯，環挾半鮫，黑室。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Kings of blood carried gold-inlaid hilts with ring mounts and black scabbard chambers.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Feudal kings carried gold-inlaid hilts with ring mounts and black scabbard chambers.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 諸侯王 means feudal kings. The accepted repair r0002 (s0150) already removed the same invented bloodline wording ("Kings of Liu blood"); this repeat also needs fixing.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 疾日嚴卯，帝令夔化，慎爾週伏，化茲靈殳。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: The summer yan-mao face adds lines commanding the spirit Kui to transform hidden banes.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: On the day of affliction, the yan-mao: the emperor commands Kui to transform them; beware, you lurking things, and be transformed by this spirit staff.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 疾日嚴卯，帝令夔化，慎爾周伏，化茲靈殳 continues the amulet inscription. The idiomatic field invents "summer" and a "face", and drops the command to the lurking things and the spirit staff.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 疾日嚴卯，帝令夔化，慎爾週伏，化茲靈殳

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 乘輿黃赤綬，四採，黃赤縹紺，淳黃圭，長二丈九尺九寸，五百首。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: The emperor’s ribbon mixed four colors on a pure yellow boss, nearly three yards long with five hundred woven “heads.”
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: The emperor’s ribbon mixed four colors on a pure yellow boss, nearly thirty feet long with five hundred woven “heads.”
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 長二丈九尺九寸 is 29.9 chi. The chapter renders chi as feet elsewhere (s0150 二丈一尺 = twenty-one feet), so "three yards" is wrong by a factor of about ten.

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 百石青紺綬，一採，宛轉繆織圭，長丈二尺。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: One hundred piculs have blue-dark shou, one hue, twisting wrongly woven gui, one zhang two chi long.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: One hundred piculs have blue-dark shou, one hue, gui woven in a twisting interlaced pattern, one zhang two chi long.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 宛轉繆織 means twisted, interlaced weaving (繆 = interwoven). It does not mean "wrongly".

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 建武、永平禁絕之，建初、永元又復中重，於是世莫能有製其裁者，乃遂絕矣。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Jianwu and Yongping utterly forbade them; Jianchu and Yongyuan again restored middle-heavy layers; then none in the age could regulate the cutting, and so they were finally cut off.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Jianwu and Yongping utterly forbade them; Jianchu and Yongyuan again restored middle-heavy layers; after that no one in the age was able to make their cut, and so they finally died out.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: 世莫能有製其裁者，乃遂絕矣 says that no one could any longer make (製) their cut, so the garments died out. It is not about regulating.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 於是世莫能有製其裁者，乃遂絕矣

definiteTranslationRepairs.chinese: 建武、永平禁絕之，建初、永元又復中重，於是世莫能有製其裁者，乃遂絕矣。
definiteTranslationRepairs.before: Early Eastern Han bans collapsed under later reigns’ fashion excess until tailors could no longer police the cuts and the court abandoned the fight.
definiteTranslationRepairs.after: Jianwu and Yongping banned these garments outright; under Jianchu and Yongyuan they came back into some use, but afterward no one could make their cut any longer, and so they finally died out.
definiteTranslationRepairs.reason: The idiomatic field says the court abandoned enforcement. The source says the garments died out because no one could make them any more (乃遂絕矣), and it drops the four named eras.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 建武、永平禁絕之，建初、永元又復中重，於是世莫能有製其裁者，乃遂絕矣

applicationOrder: Apply nativeDateRepairProposal with applyDateRepairProposal against the pinned source/extraction hashes below (the English repairs change the source hash, so apply this first).
Apply extractionEdits in order (each lists the exact before/after row).
Apply definiteTranslationRepairs through the editorial lane with an independent reviewer; refresh the compact input block (unit digests/fingerprint) mechanically.
Rerun the scoped validators and the date-audit packet; the existing research-blocked date receipt becomes stale and is replaced only by the final independent review.

after.event: While Gaozu was still obscure (高祖微時), he made a cap of bamboo skin later called the Liu clan cap; the chapter gives no year for this.

changes.reason: s0033 dates the bamboo-skin cap only to 高祖微時, Gaozu's obscure days before his rise. The BC 209-206 interval is the period after he rose in arms (and when he was already Lord of Pei and King of Han), so it contradicts 微時 rather than bounding it. The chapter supplies no year; keep the source attestation undated. Gaozu's separate BC 206 Hongmen attestation (claim-39) and his BC 206-195 hint remain.

after.event: A King of Chu once obtained a xiezhi (楚王嘗獲之) and so made the law cap; the chapter names no king and gives no date.

changes.reason: s0066 says only 楚王嘗獲之 ('a king of Chu once obtained one'). Nothing in the chapter supports the BC 400 start, and the BC 223 end is borrowed from Qin's conquest of Chu in Hu Guang's separate remark at s0068, which is not shown to concern the same king. The unidentified king's act is undated in the source.

s0068 (Hu Guang: 秦滅楚，以其君服賜執法近臣御史服之) concerns the Chu ruler at the time of Qin's conquest (其君), whose dress was given to censors. The text does not identify that ruler with the king who 'once' (嘗) obtained a xiezhi at s0066, so dating p015 to BC 223 merges two unidentified rulers. The paired non-date event claim-83 and the s0068 name/role evidence are handled in the companion identity change.

Once the conflated BC 223 conquest attestation is withdrawn, p015 is known only from the undated 楚王嘗獲之 at s0066. An empty active-date hint list is the accurate representation; keeping BC 223 would re-impose the conflation for cross-chapter identity matching.

after.event: Quoted from the Zuo Commentary: Zi Zang of Zheng loved the kingfisher cap (鄭子臧好鷸冠); the chapter gives no date.

changes.reason: The chapter quotes 鄭子臧好鷸冠 without a date. The BC 580-570 interval is also contradicted by the cited work itself: the Zuo Commentary places Zizang's love of kingfisher caps and his murder under Duke Xi 24 (636 BC), not the 580s-570s. Rather than import an outside year, keep the chapter's quotation undated.

The only chronology for p019 was the unsupported BC 580-570 interval, which conflicts with the Zuo Commentary's Duke Xi 24 (636 BC) placement. With the attestation undated, the hint must not keep the wrong window.

extractionEdits.reason: Retract: s0068 concerns the Chu ruler at Qin's conquest (其君), not shown to be the king who once (嘗) obtained a xiezhi at s0066. This companion to the date proposal's removal of claim-46 stops p015 merging two unidentified rulers.

Remove s0068 from the p015 name and role evidence. s0068 does not contain 楚王 and refers to the conquered ruler (其君), whom the chapter does not identify with p015. (Active hints are already [] after the date proposal.)

before: the king of Chu once obtained one and therefore made it
extractionEdits.reason: The English mention span at s0066 covers a whole clause carried over from accepted repair r0001. Narrow it to the referring expression only.

Drop the unsupported title name "Marquis Huiwen" (趙惠文 is King Huiwen of Zhao; no marquisate appears). Align the personal-name English form with the source-order surface "Zhao Huiwen" used in the repaired s0070 English.
English mention follows the s0070 idiomatic repair ("Zhao Huiwen crown").
English mention follows the s0099 idiomatic repair, which now names King Wuling of Zhao; the occurrence moves to the existing "King Wuling of Zhao" surface row.

s0033 dates the bamboo-skin cap only to 高祖微時, Gaozu's obscure days before his rise. 或曰周公抱成王宴居 (s0050) is an etiological anecdote. BC 1042-1030 is the conventional regency window; pre-841 BC dates are modern reconstructions. Not contradicted; keep strongly-inferred with the explicit uncertainty listed in distinctHolds.

s0066 says only 楚王嘗獲之 ('a king of Chu once obtained one'). Nothing in the chapter supports the BC 400 start, and the BC 223 end is borrowed from Qin's conquest of Chu in Hu Guang's separate remark at s0068, which is not shown to concern the same king. The unidentified king's act is undated in the source.

s0068 (Hu Guang: 秦滅楚，以其君服賜執法近臣御史服之) concerns the Chu ruler at the time of Qin's conquest (其君), whose dress was given to censors. The text does not identify that ruler with the king who 'once' (嘗) obtained a xiezhi at s0066, so dating p015 to BC 223 merges two unidentified rulers. The paired non-date event claim-83 and the s0068 name/role evidence are handled in the companion identity change.

dateAuditReceipt.summary: Complete initial source-scope chronology audit of all 204 Chinese units, 60 temporal or active-hint items, and 26 people in the Treatise on Carriages and Dress, Part Two. The chapter combines attributed compilers, legendary exempla, historical precedent, and reign-era administrative notices. Coverage is complete, but every temporal assertion remains an explicit research hold: no compiler’s writing period, ruler’s reign, or retrospective precedent is silently promoted into a person’s life span or continuous activity range.
